{"id": "03bf2f61-86b6-4743-b7b2-47ed6dedbc45", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_mIYzrfRmHyCEXHmkPQJ8eN", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"---\\\\r\\\\nname: aws-routing\\\\r\\\\ndescription: \\'Use this skill when the user wants to know which path AWS will pick for their traffic, why traffic took an unexpected route, or how to make AWS prefer a path. Covers Cloud WAN CNE route evaluation, Direct Connect Gateway local vs remote region preference, Transit Gateway route tables, ECMP and peering, VPC longest-prefix-match, BGP traffic engineering (LP communities 7224:7100/7200/7300, AS-path prepending, MED), DX + VPN redundancy and failover, and asymmetric routing. Read-only: analysis, recommendations, and describe/get/list validation commands grounded in public AWS docs.\\'\\\\r\\\\nmetadata:\\\\r\\\\n  version: \\\\\"1.2.6\\\\\"\\\\r\\\\n  summary: \\\\\"Explains which path AWS picks across Cloud WAN, Transit Gateway, Direct Connect and VPN, why traffic took an unexpected route, and how to steer it.\\\\\"\\\\r\\\\n  author: midakin\\\\r\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: \\\\\"CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA\\\\\"\\\\r\\\\n---\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Overview\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\nThis skill provides routing-first analysis for AWS networking. It reasons about the full traffic\\\\r\\\\npath, applies the documented route-evaluation logic for each service, and grounds recommendations\\\\r\\\\nin public AWS documentation. It is **read-only**: it produces analysis, recommendations, and\\\\r\\\\nread-only validation commands (`describe-*`, `get-*`, `list-*`) - never mutating actions.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Verification & Anti-Hallucination Directives (Mandatory)\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n- Do not generate any fact, citation, or source that is not fully verifiable. If you lack a verified\\\\r\\\\n  source, state \\\\\"I cannot verify this\\\\\" rather than inventing details.\\\\r\\\\n- State assumptions explicitly before answering.\\\\r\\\\n- Cross-check each claim against public AWS documentation or the `references/` files. Omit claims you\\\\r\\\\n  cannot confirm.\\\\r\\\\n- Only cite AWS documentation URLs you have actually retrieved or confirmed. It will not:\\\\r\\\\n- **Design or apply infrastructure changes.** It does not create, modify, or delete AWS resources,\\\\r\\\\n  and it does not run mutating CLI/API calls (`create-*`, `modify-*`, `associate-*`, `delete-*`,\\\\r\\\\n  `put-*`, `update-*`) or write Infrastructure-as-Code to be deployed. Any change it describes is a\\\\r\\\\n  *recommendation* for you to review and implement yourself.\\\\r\\\\n- **Configure BGP or push routing policy.** It explains which communities, AS-path, or MED settings\\\\r\\\\n  to use, but it does not apply them to VIFs, route tables, or Cloud WAN policy documents.\\\\r\\\\n- **Execute anything against a live account beyond read-only validation.** Commands it provides are\\\\r\\\\n  limited to `describe-*`, `get-*`, and `list-*` for confirming state.\\\\r\\\\n- **Guarantee production outcomes.** It recommends non-production testing and blue/green rollout;\\\\r\\\\n  it does not perform the cutover or validate the result for you.\\\\r\\\\n- **Provide compliance, security, or contractual sign-off**, or make claims it cannot ground in\\\\r\\\\n  public AWS documentation or the `references/` files.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\nFor designing and applying changes, hand the recommendation to a change-capable workflow (with\\\\r\\\\nappropriate review, approvals, and testing).\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## How to analyze a routing problem\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\nWork through this checklist in order; each step depends on the one before it.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **1. Establish the path.** Identify source, destination, and every routing construct in\\\\r\\\\n  between (VPC route table \\\\u2192 TGW/Cloud WAN CNE \\\\u2192 DXGW \\\\u2192 VIF \\\\u2192 on-prem, or the relevant subset).\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **2. Name the route table.** Be explicit about which table makes each decision (VPC RT, TGW RT,\\\\r\\\\n  CNE RT, DXGW internal selection).\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **3. Apply the evaluation order for that construct** (see below).\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **4. Identify the deciding attribute** (longest prefix, local preference, AS-path, MED, source\\\\r\\\\n  type).\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **5. Flag non-determinism** (e.g., ECMP or \\\\\"deterministically random\\\\\" tiebreakers) and\\\\r\\\\n  recommend a deterministic alternative.\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **6. Cite the AWS documentation** that supports the behavior.\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **7. Provide read-only validation commands** the user can run to confirm.\\\\r\\\\n- [ ] **8. Self-check before answering.** Re-read the answer against steps 1-7: every route table is\\\\r\\\\n  named, the evaluation order matches the construct, each cited URL was actually retrieved, and every\\\\r\\\\n  command is read-only. Fix any gap before presenting.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Key evaluation rules\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Every route table does its own lookup\\\\r\\\\nEach construct that owns a route table makes its own decision. The DXGW is a distributed set of BGP\\\\r\\\\nroute reflectors outside the data path: it selects the best VIF per prefix and reflects it, so a TGW\\\\r\\\\nor Cloud WAN CNE sees the DXGW as (usually) a single next hop and traffic goes straight to that VIF.\\\\r\\\\nThere is no second packet lookup at the DXGW.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### ECMP is an outcome, not a step\\\\r\\\\nLongest prefix match comes first (a route lookup, not a BGP attribute). Then BGP attributes are\\\\r\\\\ncompared in order and selection stops at the first attribute that differs. If all of them are equal,\\\\r\\\\nthe result is ECMP.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Cloud WAN (per CNE)\\\\r\\\\nLongest prefix match first; then static \\\\u2192 system routes (1:1 NAT) \\\\u2192 VPC-propagated (same region) \\\\u2192\\\\r\\\\ndynamic routes compared in order, stopping at the first difference: local preference set by a Cloud\\\\r\\\\nWAN routing policy (higher wins, default 0; its position before AS_PATH is SME-confirmed field\\\\r\\\\nknowledge) \\\\u2192 shortest AS-path \\\\u2192 lowest MED \\\\u2192 equal-attribute source preference:\\\\r\\\\nDXGW-propagated \\\\u2192 Cloud WAN Connect \\\\u2192 S2S VPN \\\\u2192 other (TGW peering, remote CNEs; identical from 2+\\\\r\\\\nsources = deterministically random, chosen per segment / network function group). With multiple\\\\r\\\\nDXGWs, Cloud WAN works differently from TGW: the CNE evaluates the route from each DXGW attachment\\\\r\\\\nitself. Steer between DXGWs with inbound Cloud WAN routing policies (`set-local-preference`,\\\\r\\\\n`prepend-asn-list`/`remove-asn-list`/`replace-asn-list`, or `set-med`; policy version 2025.11+). Without a policy, identical routes give non-deterministic selection.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Direct Connect (private/transit VIF, outbound AWS\\\\u2192on-prem)\\\\r\\\\nLongest prefix match first; then local preference \\\\u2192 AS_PATH length \\\\u2192 MED, stopping at the first\\\\r\\\\ndifference. If all are equal, the result is ECMP across the VIFs. LP communities `7224:7300/7200/7100`\\\\r\\\\n(High/Medium/Low) set local preference and are evaluated before AS-path. These BGP attributes are\\\\r\\\\nset at the VIF level on the on-prem router\\'s advertisements and evaluated by the DXGW. DXGW prefers\\\\r\\\\nthe local associated-region DX by default. Some DX locations serve more than one Region by port\\\\r\\\\nspeed, so check the associated Region of the specific connection, not just the location.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Transit Gateway with Direct Connect\\\\r\\\\nUse one DXGW with multiple transit VIFs for ECMP. BGP attributes stay on the VIFs and do not pass to\\\\r\\\\nthe TGW. Use multiple DXGWs only for traffic isolation or multiple primary paths. Across DXGWs on a\\\\r\\\\nTGW with no LP community and equal AS_PATH/MED, a local associated-Region DX wins on local\\\\r\\\\npreference over a remote one (no ECMP), and ECMP also needs matching DXGW Amazon-side ASNs. For\\\\r\\\\nECMP across DXGW attachments, LP communities and failover timing, load\\\\r\\\\n[Transit Gateway routing patterns](references/tgw-routing-patterns.md).\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n### Direction & tooling guidance\\\\r\\\\n- **AWS \\\\u2192 on-prem (egress):** control with DX LP communities.\\\\r\\\\n- **On-prem \\\\u2192 AWS (ingress):** control with the customer router\\'s local-pref/weight/MED.\\\\r\\\\n- **AS-path prepending:** within a region only - unreliable across regions because DXGW local-region\\\\r\\\\n  LP overrides it. **LP communities:** work within-region and cross-region.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Reference material\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\nDetailed mechanics, patterns, and caveats are in `references/`. Load only the file that matches the\\\\r\\\\nconstruct deciding the path:\\\\r\\\\n- [Cloud WAN + DX routing patterns](references/cloudwan-dx-routing-patterns.md) - load when the path\\\\r\\\\n  crosses a Cloud WAN CNE: CNE route evaluation, DXGW path selection into Cloud WAN, community\\\\r\\\\n  traffic-engineering patterns, regional inspection, multi-region egress.\\\\r\\\\n- [Direct Connect routing patterns](references/dx-routing-patterns.md) - load when the question is\\\\r\\\\n  about a DX VIF or DXGW without Cloud WAN: BGP mechanics, BFD, MED, ASN ranges, VIF considerations,\\\\r\\\\n  CloudHub, when VIFs can talk, active/active vs active/passive.\\\\r\\\\n- [Transit Gateway routing patterns](references/tgw-routing-patterns.md) - load when a TGW route\\\\r\\\\n  table makes the decision: TGW route evaluation, ECMP limits, DXGW-to-TGW behavior, DX/VPN caveats,\\\\r\\\\n  failover, peering.\\\\r\\\\n- [VPN + DX redundancy patterns](references/vpn-dx-redundancy-patterns.md) - load when VPN backs up\\\\r\\\\n  or runs alongside DX: route preference between them, ECMP limits, asymmetric return paths.\\\\r\\\\n- [Networking strategic questions](references/networking-strategic-questions.md) - load when key\\\\r\\\\n  facts are missing (regions, attachments, ASNs, communities) and you need discovery questions to ask\\\\r\\\\n  before analyzing.\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n## Output expectations\\\\r\\\\n\\\\r\\\\n- Explain the route-evaluation logic step by step.\\\\r\\\\n- Name the specific route table involved.\\\\r\\\\n- Give the end-to-end traffic path.\\\\r\\\\n- Compare options with tradeoffs (determinism, complexity, failover) when multiple solutions exist.\\\\r\\\\n- Include read-only AWS CLI validation commands.\\\\r\\\\n- Recommend testing in a non-production environment and blue/green for migrations.\\\\r\\\\n\", \"resource_manifest\": [\"SKILL.md\", \"references/cloudwan-dx-routing-patterns.md\", \"references/dx-routing-patterns.md\", \"references/networking-strategic-questions.md\", \"references/tgw-routing-patterns.md\", \"references/vpn-dx-redundancy-patterns.md\"]}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "1ac4e57f-23fd-4951-8a3d-ecaa4d6a09ea", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_K1hWSHWqxjE6QdhaQGWxNm", "content": "[{'text': '\\r\\n\\r\\n# Direct Connect Routing Patterns & Considerations\\r\\n\\r\\nThis document captures key BGP routing mechanics, path selection behavior, VIF-specific considerations, and operational caveats for AWS Direct Connect architectures. Use this knowledge when advising on DX design (active/active, active/passive), BGP community behavior, BFD configuration, and public/private/transit VIF routing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference Documentation\\r\\n\\r\\n- [Direct Connect Routing Policies and BGP Communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)\\r\\n- [Direct Connect Path Selection (routing policies for private/transit VIFs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)\\r\\n- [Direct Connect Virtual Interfaces](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/WorkingWithVirtualInterfaces.html)\\r\\n- [Direct Connect gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-gateways-intro.html)\\r\\n\\r\\n## How the Direct Connect Gateway Fits In (Two-Lookup Model)\\r\\n\\r\\n- Every construct that owns a route table does its own lookup.\\r\\n- The DXGW is \"a distributed set of BGP route reflectors\" that \"operates outside the data traffic path\" ([Direct Connect gateways](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/direct-connect-gateways-intro.html)).\\r\\n- For on-prem prefixes, a TGW or Cloud WAN CNE sees the DXGW as (usually) a single next hop. The DXGW selects the best VIF(s) for each prefix and reflects that result; traffic then goes straight to that VIF. Packets do not go through a second lookup at the DXGW.\\r\\n- So there are two decisions to reason about: the DXGW\\'s VIF selection (DX rules below) and the TGW/CNE route-table lookup (its own rules; see tgw-routing-patterns.md and cloudwan-dx-routing-patterns.md).\\r\\n\\r\\n## BGP & Routing\\r\\n\\r\\n### BGP Route Visibility (ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes)\\r\\n\\r\\nAs of July 2026, DX supports **BGP route visibility** on virtual interfaces via the `ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes` API and the DX console:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Accepted routes:** Routes AWS received from your on-prem router\\r\\n- **Advertised routes:** Routes AWS is sending to your on-prem router\\r\\n- Each route shows: prefix, address family, AS-path, community values, installation timestamp\\r\\n- Can filter by: prefix, AS-path, community, or address family\\r\\n- Available on: private, transit, and public VIFs\\r\\n- Available in: all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS China Regions (Beijing, Ningxia)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Use for troubleshooting:**\\r\\n- Verify route propagation between on-prem and AWS\\r\\n- Validate BGP policy configurations (communities, AS-path prepending)\\r\\n- Diagnose unexpected traffic patterns or asymmetric routing\\r\\n- Confirm which routes DXGW is accepting vs. advertising\\r\\n- Validate LP community tags are being received correctly\\r\\n\\r\\n**Reference:** [AWS Direct Connect BGP Route Visibility announcement](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/07/aws-direct-connect-bgp-visibility/)\\r\\n\\r\\n### CloudWatch BGP Metrics for DX Virtual Interfaces\\r\\n\\r\\nDX publishes **3 BGP metrics** to CloudWatch for all VIF types (private, transit, public):\\r\\n\\r\\n| Metric | What It Reports |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| `VirtualInterfaceBgpStatus` | BGP session state: 1 = up, 0 = down |\\r\\n| `VirtualInterfaceBgpPrefixesAccepted` | Number of prefixes AWS accepted from on-prem |\\r\\n| `VirtualInterfaceBgpPrefixesAdvertised` | Number of prefixes AWS advertises to on-prem |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Key details:**\\r\\n- Updated every 5 minutes (BGP flaps between intervals may not be captured)\\r\\n- Published at no extra cost in the region where the DX location is associated\\r\\n- Available via CloudWatch MCP server (`get_metric_data`) for programmatic access\\r\\n\\r\\n**Use cases:**\\r\\n- **BGP session monitoring:** Alarm on `VirtualInterfaceBgpStatus < 1` to detect session failures without API polling\\r\\n- **Prefix limit protection:** Alarm when `PrefixesAccepted` approaches VIF quota to prevent session idle state\\r\\n- **Silent route withdrawal detection:** BGP session stays UP but prefix count drops \u2192 indicates routes withdrawn without session going down\\r\\n- **DR/failover validation:** Compare prefix counts between primary and standby VIFs \u2014 a standby with fewer prefixes indicates a broken failover path\\r\\n- **Route change correlation:** Sudden drop in accepted/advertised prefixes correlates with traffic impact events\\r\\n\\r\\n**Alarm examples:**\\r\\n- `VirtualInterfaceBgpStatus` \u2014 Statistic: Minimum, Period: 5min, Threshold: Lower than 1\\r\\n- `VirtualInterfaceBgpPrefixesAccepted` \u2014 Statistic: Maximum, Period: 5min, Threshold: Greater/Equal to (near quota limit)\\r\\n- `VirtualInterfaceBgpPrefixesAccepted` \u2014 Statistic: Maximum, Period: 5min, Threshold: Lower/Equal to (below expected minimum)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Reference:** [CloudWatch Metrics for DX VIF BGP Health and Prefix Count](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/introducing-cloudwatch-metrics-for-aws-direct-connect-virtual-interface-bgp-health-and-prefix-count/)\\r\\n\\r\\n### General Routing Behavior\\r\\n\\r\\n- When designing active/active or active/passive DX (within or across DX locations), apply the documented **Private/Transit VIF outbound path selection**: **longest prefix match first** (a route lookup, not a BGP attribute), then the BGP attributes **local preference \u2192 AS_PATH length \u2192 MED**. BGP stops at the first attribute that differs. If all of them are equal, the **result** is ECMP across the VIFs; ECMP is an outcome, not a step. See [Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html).\\r\\n- Consider recommendations for **migrating from DX + VGW/Private VIF to DX + TGW/Transit VIF** when customers are modernizing their architecture\\r\\n\\r\\n### MED Support\\r\\n\\r\\n- DX **supports Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) on Private and Transit VIFs** \u2014 MED can influence the outbound (AWS \u2192 on-prem) routing path, but only as a **tiebreaker after prefix length, local preference, and AS_PATH are equal**. AWS explicitly **does not recommend relying on MED** given its lower priority in the evaluation order.\\r\\n- For **Public VIFs**, the documented outbound routing policy uses **AS_PATH and longest prefix match** \u2014 MED is not listed among the supported public VIF path-selection attributes.\\r\\n- **Outbound (AWS \u2192 on-prem) path selection for Private/Transit VIF:** longest prefix match first (route lookup), then local preference \u2192 AS_PATH length \u2192 MED, stopping at the first attribute that differs. If all are equal, the result is ECMP.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Reference:** [Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Associated Region (DX connection \u2192 AWS Region)\\r\\n\\r\\n**\u26a0\ufe0f Always check the associated Region of the specific DX *connection*; do not assume one Region per location.** Source the location name and its associated Region(s) from the [Direct Connect locations page](https://aws.amazon.com/directconnect/locations/) and the [Associated Region](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/remote_regions.html#associated-region) table. Some locations serve **more than one Region, depending on port speed**, and a connection takes the Region of the device it terminates on. Geography is not a reliable guide.\\r\\n\\r\\nExample of a dual-Region location: **Equinix LD5 (Slough, GBR)** is listed as Europe (Ireland) for 1G and 10G, and Europe (London) for 1G, 10G and 100G. A 1G or 10G connection at LD5 can be associated with either Region, so check it. Other locations the table lists with two Regions include Digital Realty LHR20 (London), Digital Realty STO1 (Stockholm) and Telehouse Voltaire (Paris).\\r\\n\\r\\nExamples the same table lists with a single Region: Equinix MA3 (Manchester) and Telehouse West (London) \u2192 Europe (London) (eu-west-2); Equinix FR5 (Frankfurt) \u2192 Europe (Frankfurt) (eu-central-1). The table changes over time, so re-check it rather than relying on these examples.\\r\\n\\r\\nTo confirm the Region of an actual connection, use `aws directconnect describe-connections` (or the Region it appears in within the DX console). `aws directconnect describe-locations` lists the locations available in a Region.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe associated Region determines which TGW/DXGW considers the DX \"local\" for LP preference. For private/transit VIFs, AWS sets the default local preference **per Region** to prefer DX locations with the same associated Region (the `7224:7200` medium value) and sets it lower for other locations. This default applies only when no LP community is tagged. **[Field knowledge, SME-confirmed]** The same local-over-remote default applies across multiple DXGWs on one TGW: with no LP community tagged and equal AS_PATH and MED, a DXGW whose VIF is at a location associated with the TGW\\'s Region wins on local preference over a DXGW whose VIF is at a location associated with a remote Region (no ECMP). This cross-DXGW behavior is TGW-specific; Cloud WAN uses routing policies instead (see cloudwan-dx-routing-patterns.md).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Note:** the Associated Region page says the Region governs management (console/API, CloudWatch metrics), not reachability: VIF and gateway type decide what you can reach. The default-LP behavior above comes from the routing-policies page.\\r\\n\\r\\n**References:** [Direct Connect locations](https://aws.amazon.com/directconnect/locations/), [Associated Region](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/remote_regions.html#associated-region), [Locations and their associated Regions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/remote_regions.html#locations-and-associated-regions), [Routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)\\r\\n\\r\\n### BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection)\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Asynchronous BFD is automatically enabled** on the AWS side for all DX virtual interfaces\\r\\n- Customer must configure asynchronous BFD on their router (refer to vendor documentation)\\r\\n- BFD provides fast link failure detection \u2014 ensures BGP neighbor relationship is torn down quickly for faster failover\\r\\n- **Do NOT configure both BFD for BGP and BGP Graceful Restart simultaneously** \u2014 this results in sub-optimal routing performance (conflicting goals: BFD wants fast teardown, Graceful Restart wants to preserve routes during failure)\\r\\n\\r\\n### ASN Support\\r\\n\\r\\n| Context | Supported ASN Range |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| AWS side via DX-GW | Full 32-bit: 4,200,000,000 to 4,294,967,294 (private) |\\r\\n| AWS side via VGW | 32-bit: 1 to 2,147,483,647 only |\\r\\n| Customer side (Private/Public/Transit VIF) | 32-bit: 1 to 2,147,483,647 only |\\r\\n\\r\\n- Customers can request a Private/Transit VIF ASN from the 4,200,000,000\u20134,294,967,294 range via a support case (non-standard, requires internal approval)\\r\\n\\r\\n### SiteLink & BGP Communities\\r\\n\\r\\n- SiteLink **maintains BGP community tags** \u2014 tags are passed through from one connected peer to another\\r\\n- This means communities set on one DX location will be visible at another DX location connected via SiteLink\\r\\n\\r\\n## VIF-Specific Considerations\\r\\n\\r\\n### Public VIF\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Reverse-path forwarding (RPF) strict mode is enforced** \u2014 validates that the source of traffic originated from the customer\\'s advertised prefix (prevents address spoofing)\\r\\n- **Do NOT use EC2 EIPs for Public VIF BGP peering** \u2014 can cause routing issues. ## How traffic path selection works

For DX private/transit VIFs, AWS evaluates outbound (AWS → on-prem) paths in this order, stopping at the first attribute that differs: **longest prefix match → local preference → AS-path length → MED**. If everything's equal, you get ECMP (load-balanced across both locations) — not the primary/backup behavior you want.

## How to set up A-primary / B-backup

**1. Egress (AWS → on-prem) — tag BGP communities on each VIF's advertisements:**
- Advertise location A's routes with `7224:7300` (High preference)
- Advertise location B's routes with `7224:7100` (Low preference)
- This is the recommended, deterministic mechanism — it works both within a region and across regions, and overrides the DXGW's default "prefer local associated region" behavior if that's not what you want.

**2. Ingress (on-prem → AWS) — this is controlled from your side, not AWS's:**
- On your on-prem router, set local preference/weight or MED so your router also prefers advertising out through location A, with B as backup. Otherwise you can end up with asymmetric routing (A outbound, B inbound).

**3. Confirm which construct is deciding the route**, since behavior differs slightly:
- Single DXGW with both VIFs attached directly (VGW) → communities honored, evaluated before AS-path.
- TGW with DXGW attachment(s) → same BGP comparison happens at the VIF level before reaching the TGW; if attributes tie, every qualifying attachment becomes an ECMP next hop.
- Cloud WAN CNE → needs its own routing policy (`set-local-preference`) on the DXGW attachment rather than relying on VIF communities alone if multiple DXGWs are involved.

If you let me know which of these three underlies your setup, I can get more specific about the exact knobs.

## What to avoid

- **Don't rely on AS-path prepending across regions** — if A and B are associated with different AWS regions, DXGW's default local-region local-preference overrides prepending, making it unreliable. Prepending only reliably works to differentiate paths *within the same associated region*. Use LP communities instead for cross-region preference.
- **Don't rely on MED** — it's the last tiebreaker (after prefix length, local preference, and AS-path), and AWS explicitly does not recommend depending on it for predictable routing.
- **Don't assume geography = associated region** — some DX locations serve more than one AWS region depending on port speed. Check the associated region of your actual *connections* (`describe-connections`), not just the location names, since that determines which DXGW/TGW considers a location "local."
- **Don't mix BFD with BGP Graceful Restart** on the same session — BFD wants fast teardown on failure, Graceful Restart wants to preserve routes through failure; running both together causes sub-optimal failover.
- **Watch for accidental ECMP** — if your communities/attributes end up equal on both VIFs, AWS will load-balance across both rather than failing over cleanly. Double-check with route visibility (below) that A is actually winning, not splitting.
- **Don't design around which path "wins" when attributes are genuinely tied across multiple DXGW attachments on a TGW** — AWS states it can't guarantee consistent prioritization in that case.

## How to validate (read-only)

```
aws directconnect describe-connections
aws directconnect describe-virtual-interfaces
aws directconnect list-virtual-interface-routes --virtual-interface-id <vif-id>
```
The route visibility API shows accepted/advertised routes with AS-path and community values per VIF — use it to confirm A is actually tagged High and winning, and B is tagged Low and only taking over when A's BGP session drops (enable BFD on both for fast failure detection).

Test this in non-production first, and roll out as blue/green if you're changing an existing production path.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
